metadata.scope: Tactical and sport-IQ knowledge only. Stroke mechanics, strength exercise instruction, and generic conditioning detail are included only when they alter tactical choices, match reading, load risk, or training transfer.
metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready badminton knowledge for scoring pressure, serve and receive, first three shots, singles rally construction, doubles and mixed doubles systems, attacking and defensive formations, opponent-position shot selection, deception, tempo control, match-week adjustments, level teaching, physical-tactical demands, load risk, training implications, and records to create.
metadata.rule_context_note: As of 2026-06-21, retain configurable scoring profiles because the existing 21-point rally system remains central in coaching resources while BWF has announced a 3x15 system effective 2027. Backend scoring-pressure logic should not hard-code one score map.

key_concepts.name: Score Pressure Is Phase-Based
key_concepts.summary: Rally scoring makes every rally a scoring event, but the tactical meaning of a point changes across early exploration, middle separation, end-game pressure, deuce, and match-point states.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Players need a score-state plan: learn early, protect the middle-game margin, reduce low-percentage errors late, and make serve/receive routines more deliberate at game point.

key_concepts.name: The First Phase Is an Information Race
key_concepts.summary: The first points are not just warm-up. They reveal serve comfort, backhand corner tolerance, net courage, lift quality, recovery habits, and emotional response to pressure.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Use the first 5 to 7 rallies to test a small set of probes, not to gamble randomly.

key_concepts.name: Serve and Receive Shape the Rally Before It Opens
key_concepts.summary: The serve and receive phase establishes who wins time, who controls height, and which player or pair must lift first.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Train serve, receive, and third-shot decisions as one unit, not as isolated technical drills.

key_concepts.name: The First Three Shots Are a Tactical Contract
key_concepts.summary: Serve, return, and third shot decide whether the rally begins as attack, neutral, or defense. In doubles and mixed doubles this phase often decides front-court ownership and the chance to attack first.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Code first-three outcomes as attack_created, neutral_kept, forced_lift, lifted_under_pressure, or error.

key_concepts.name: Attack, Neutral, and Defense Are Decision States
key_concepts.summary: Badminton tactics become clearer when every contact is classified by the player's pressure state rather than by shot name alone.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: A drop from balance can be attacking; the same drop when late can be a defensive escape. Store the pressure state with the shot.

key_concepts.name: Win Space and Win Time
key_concepts.summary: Sport IQ in badminton is the ability to make the opponent cover more court and react later while the player or pair recovers to a better base.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Evaluate a shot by the next base, opponent contact quality, and likely reply, not only whether the shuttle landed in.

key_concepts.name: Singles Rally Construction Balances Moving, Pinning, and Finishing
key_concepts.summary: Singles rallies are built by combining width, depth, height, and tempo to move the opponent, pin weak recovery patterns, and create finishing chances without forcing the attack too early.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Track patterns such as rear-corner pin to net, straight clear to cross drop, body smash to net follow, and reset clear after late contact.

key_concepts.name: Doubles Rotation Is Continuous
key_concepts.summary: Doubles attack and defense are not fixed positions. Pairs rotate between front-back attack, side-by-side defense, and transitional shapes based on shuttle height, opponent lift quality, and who is moving forward or backward.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Teach who follows, who covers, and when to switch using shuttle height and player momentum cues.

key_concepts.name: Mixed Doubles Roles Are Responsibilities, Not Stereotypes
key_concepts.summary: Mixed doubles often uses a front-court controller and rear-court pressure role, but the tactical rule is responsibility by shuttle, skill, balance, and opponent response rather than gender alone.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Store mixed roles as front_court_control, midcourt_intercept, rear_court_attack, serve_receive_pressure, and emergency_rotation rather than fixed player labels.

key_concepts.name: Formation Depends on Shuttle Height
key_concepts.summary: A high shuttle to the pair in balance supports front-back attack; a fast flat exchange may require staggered midcourt coverage; a forced lift or smash defense usually moves the pair toward side-by-side coverage.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Use formation transitions as a drill target: attack shape, neutral drive shape, defense shape, counterattack conversion.

key_concepts.name: Shot Selection Starts With Opponent Position and Balance
key_concepts.summary: The best shot is the one that punishes opponent location, body shape, recovery direction, and likely expectation while staying within the player's contact quality.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Teach reads: opponent deep equals net threat; opponent creeping equals fast lift or push; opponent leaning cross equals straight hold; opponent late at backhand equals keep them turning.

key_concepts.name: Deception Controls Information
key_concepts.summary: Deception works when preparation, contact timing, and tactical context delay the opponent's read without making the player late or unstable.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Begin with hold-and-hit options from balance, then add opponent-specific disguise once the base shot is reliable.

key_concepts.name: Tempo Is a Pressure Lever
key_concepts.summary: Pace, pause, height, and early interception change the opponent's available time. Fast tempo can rush a weaker defender; slower height can recover base or disrupt an opponent who expects pace.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Teach tempo changes intentionally: speed up to punish late recovery, slow down to reset, vary pace to hide the next acceleration.

key_concepts.name: Observation Must Become a Small Adjustment
key_concepts.summary: Effective match IQ turns observation into one or two usable changes, such as serve target, receive shape, smash placement, lift height, or doubles rotation cue.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Use match notes under space, strengths, weaknesses, psychology, winners, errors, and patterns leading to errors.

key_concepts.name: Tournament Coaching Is Individualized
key_concepts.summary: Some athletes need direct instruction, some need questions, some need emotional regulation, and some need minimal input during matches.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Backend plans should store athlete feedback preference and match-week communication rules.

key_concepts.name: Format-Specific Demands Change Tactics and Training
key_concepts.summary: Singles, doubles, and mixed doubles differ in rally structure, shot frequency, movement demands, and tactical emphasis, so the same drill can be wrong if it ignores the target event.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: Tag every tactical drill by event format and expected decision speed.

key_concepts.name: Load Risk Limits Tactical Choices
key_concepts.summary: Late lunges, jump-smash landings, direction changes, high-speed backcourt movement, and repeated overhead attacks can shift the best tactical choice from aggressive to controlled.
key_concepts.coaching_translation: When fatigue or pain rises, use tactics that preserve court control without repeatedly forcing the same high-risk movement.

states.primary_intent: Discover opponent patterns while avoiding careless streaks.
preferred_decisions: test deep backhand and forehand corners
avoid: three repeated errors before changing plan
giving back points after winning a long rally
changing a working pattern without cause

states.primary_intent: Keep tactical clarity while pressure rises.
preferred_decisions: make opponent play one more quality shot
attack when contact quality is high
avoid: rushing the rally because of score anxiety

states.primary_intent: Use rehearsed pressure routines and avoid ambiguous plans.
avoid: low-percentage line winners from late contact

technical_models.name: Serve and Receive Tactical Model

serve_intents.primary_goal: Deny attack and invite a predictable net, lift, or push reply.
third_shot_plan: prepare rear player to attack lifted return

serve_intents.primary_goal: Punish receiver creep and disrupt an aggressive front-foot receive stance.
third_shot_plan: expect smash/drop from receiver if flick is short
reset if lift quality is poor

serve_intents.primary_goal: Push singles receiver back, test overhead consistency, and create time for base.
third_shot_plan: prepare to defend steep attack if serve sits short

serve_intents.primary_goal: Rush receiver hands and jam preferred receive pattern.

receive_intents: return to make server lift or move away from preferred third shot
vary net, push, lift, and drive based on server stance and partner coverage
avoid giving the serving pair a free front-court kill

sequence.decision_question: What response do we want, and what response must we cover?
Can we seize time or force the server/pair to lift?
Do we attack, neutralize, or defend the receiver's reply?

layers.decision_focus: Can the player recover to a base that covers the most likely replies?
Can the player force width, depth, or front-back movement without losing balance?
Should this shot rush, pause, lift, flatten, or reset?
Is the contact and opponent position good enough to finish, or should the player keep constructing?

technical_models.name: Doubles Rotation Model

responsibilities: front_player cuts blocks and loose drives
front player avoids blocking rear player's sightline
lift high enough only when needed
look for counter-drive or net block to change state
one player shades forward to intercept
avoid both players chasing same drive

rotation_rules: Player moving forward after a good drop or block usually continues forward unless partner is better positioned.
Player pushed backward after a lift usually becomes rear-court defender or attacker depending on shuttle height.
A pair should rotate because of shuttle and momentum, not because of a pre-decided loop.

technical_models.name: Mixed Doubles Role Model

success_signals: keeps racket up after partner attack

tasks: choose placements that feed front player
success_signals: does not over-smash into prepared defense
uses drop and stick smash to change rhythm

tasks: cover when front player is lifted over
reset shape with high clear or controlled block

constraints: Do not hard-code gender; store handedness, strengths, speed, front-court skill, rear-court power, and receive quality.
Train both players in emergency opposite-role tasks.

technical_models.name: Shot Selection by Opponent Position Matrix

reads.risk_warning: Avoid delicate net shot if own recovery is poor and opponent is fast forward.
Do not feed a loose net kill to an opponent already on top of the tape.
Cross-court winners are lower value if contact is late and center recovery is exposed.
Full-power smash into prepared defense can donate counterattack.
Overplaying the open sideline may miss when a simple seam shot would win time.

technical_models.name: Deception Decision Model
requirements: same preparation for at least two options

deception_types.best_use: At net or midcourt when opponent commits early.
deception_types.risk: Holding too long converts attack to late defense.

deception_types.best_use: From overhead balance to change shuttle speed and direction.
deception_types.risk: Thin contact can float if player chases disguise before quality.

deception_types.best_use: When opponent reads shoulders or racket face early.
Slow-fast contrast after opponent settles into rhythm.
deception_types.risk: Predictable pauses become attack cues for strong opponents.

tempo_tools.effect: Buys recovery time or changes attack angle.
Breaks defender rhythm and forces a new split-step timing.
Compresses time in doubles and attacks body/seams.

defensive_outputs.intent: Survive and recover when under severe pressure.
defensive_outputs.counterattack_path: Force opponent to hit again from backcourt, then look for lower-quality next attack.

defensive_outputs.intent: Convert smash defense into front-court pressure.
defensive_outputs.counterattack_path: If opponent is deep after smash, block tight and move forward.

defensive_outputs.intent: Rush an attacker whose recovery or racket preparation is poor.
defensive_outputs.counterattack_path: Aim body or seam in doubles; aim hip or open side in singles.

defensive_outputs.intent: Use angle only when the attacker's partner or recovery leaves space.
defensive_outputs.counterattack_path: Create open court but account for longer shuttle path and own recovery.

technical_models.name: Tournament and Match-Week Tactical Adjustment Model

avoid: changing every pattern after one bad game

technical_models.name: Beginner to Advanced Tactical Teaching Model

indicators.definition: Net advantage created within first three shots minus first-three errors.
Rate at which a player or pair forces the opponent to lift from serve-return, net play, or pressure attack.
Points or clear advantage won after obtaining downward attack.
Percentage of defensive contacts that reset neutral or create counterattack rather than donate another attack.
Doubles or mixed rallies without avoidable collision, same-shuttle chase, uncovered seam, or delayed formation switch.
Unforced or decision errors by score state, especially after intervals, at 16-plus, and at game or match point.

tactical_rules.rule: If the game is in the early score band, use planned probes to test opponent weaknesses while keeping error cost low.
tactical_rules.rationale: Early points provide information and prevent the opponent from building confidence through cheap errors.

tactical_rules.rule: If a player or pair creates a middle-game lead, continue the pattern that created it until the opponent makes a clear adjustment.
tactical_rules.rationale: The middle band is where winning players often turn small reads into meaningful separation.

tactical_rules.rule: At 16-plus or deuce, choose rehearsed serve-return and rally patterns before attempting new deception or untested winners.
tactical_rules.rationale: Pressure magnifies indecision and technical miss risk.

tactical_rules.rule: Every serve should have a named expected return and a named third-shot answer.
tactical_rules.rationale: Serve quality is incomplete without coverage of the most likely reply.

tactical_rules.rule: After a low serve in doubles or mixed, the serving pair must cover the fast push as carefully as the net reply.
tactical_rules.rationale: Receivers who cannot win the tape may still win time by pushing into the midcourt or rear seam.

tactical_rules.rule: Use the flick serve only when receiver creep is visible and the server or pair has a defensive plan if the flick is attacked.
tactical_rules.rationale: A surprise serve that creates a weak lift is valuable; a short flick gives the opponent first attack.

tactical_rules.rule: If the receiver is balanced and can contact early, prioritize replies that force the server or pair to lift or defend.
tactical_rules.rationale: Early receive contact wins time and can decide the front-court battle before the rally develops.

tactical_rules.rule: Tag every serve-return-third-shot sequence by tactical outcome, not only by shot used.
tactical_rules.rationale: The useful coaching question is whether the sequence created attack, neutralized, or conceded pressure.

tactical_rules.rule: In singles, attack fully only when contact quality and opponent position support it; otherwise keep moving the opponent and improving the next shot.
tactical_rules.rationale: Premature winners from poor positions often open counterattack or create fatigue without reward.

tactical_rules.rule: If the opponent is deep and still recovering backward, threaten the front court unless their forward speed or your poor balance makes the drop unsafe.
tactical_rules.rationale: Depth opens front-court space, but only if the player can recover after the shot.

tactical_rules.rule: If the opponent is creeping forward, use depth, body speed, or flat push to punish the forward commitment.
tactical_rules.rationale: Opponent court position is a more important cue than a favorite shot list.

tactical_rules.rule: If a defender is balanced and waiting for a sideline smash, attack the body, hip, racket shoulder, or use a pace change before going for the line.
tactical_rules.rationale: Body pressure reduces counter angles and can produce weak blocks.

tactical_rules.rule: Use cross-court attacking shots only when contact is early enough to recover and the opponent's recovery direction creates value.
tactical_rules.rationale: Cross-court shots travel farther and can expose the straight counter if played late.

tactical_rules.rule: When a pair earns downward attack from a lift, move into front-back shape with one player creating pressure and the other hunting weak replies.
tactical_rules.rationale: Front-back attack divides finishing and interception tasks.

tactical_rules.rule: When a pair is forced to lift and the opponent has downward attack, recover toward side-by-side coverage unless a specific staggered defense is planned.
tactical_rules.rationale: Side-by-side defense protects body, tramline, and seam against smash and fast drop pressure.

tactical_rules.rule: If a smash block forces the attacker forward from deep court, the blocker or partner should prepare to move in and challenge the next net shot.
tactical_rules.rationale: Good defense should look for transition, not only survival.

tactical_rules.rule: The player whose shot and momentum take them forward usually owns the next front-court responsibility unless partner position clearly overrides it.
tactical_rules.rationale: Rotation that follows momentum is faster and reduces collision risk.

tactical_rules.rule: If both partners move toward the same shuttle, the pair must have a communication or priority rule based on forehand side, front player, or better balance.
tactical_rules.rationale: Avoidable same-shuttle chasing opens the opposite court and increases collision risk.

tactical_rules.rule: Rear-court attacks in mixed should often be placed to create blocks and interceptions for the front-court controller, not only to hit winners.
tactical_rules.rationale: Mixed attack is strongest when rear pressure and front interception work as one pattern.

tactical_rules.rule: Mixed pairs must train emergency role inversion when the front player is lifted over or the rear player is pulled forward.
tactical_rules.rationale: Strong opponents target fixed role assumptions; survival depends on temporary role competence.

tactical_rules.rule: Use deception from balanced contact before using it from late or stretched positions.
tactical_rules.rationale: Disguise loses value if it costs recovery, accuracy, or tactical state.

tactical_rules.rule: Do not teach a deceptive option until the visible base shot is good enough to be respected.
tactical_rules.rationale: Opponents are deceived by credible alternatives, not by random racket movement.

tactical_rules.rule: If contact is late or balance is poor, use height, depth, or safer placement to recover before re-accelerating the rally.
tactical_rules.rationale: Tactical patience preserves the next decision and reduces forced errors.

tactical_rules.rule: If the opponent is late, off balance, or wrong-footed, take the shuttle earlier or flatter to remove recovery time.
tactical_rules.rationale: Winning time is often more valuable than adding power.

tactical_rules.rule: During a match, reduce observations to the two or three factors most likely to change outcome.
tactical_rules.rationale: Too much information between rallies or games can reduce execution clarity.

tactical_rules.rule: After an interval, open with a clear serve-return or rally pattern that confirms the adjustment rather than improvising.
tactical_rules.rationale: Intervals interrupt rhythm and are useful only if the player returns with a simple plan.

tactical_rules.rule: In match week, sharpen existing tactical menus instead of installing complex new patterns.
tactical_rules.rationale: Tournament readiness depends on confidence, repeatability, and freshness.

tactical_rules.rule: If shuttle speed, drift, lighting, or floor grip changes, adjust height, margin, serve depth, and jump-smash risk before judging form.
tactical_rules.rationale: Environmental context changes tactical value and error rates.

tactical_rules.rule: When fatigue causes late split steps, rushed recovery, or repeated poor lunges, shift from maximal attack to higher-margin patterns until movement quality returns.
tactical_rules.rationale: Fatigue changes both decision accuracy and injury risk.

physical_demands.name: Intermittent High-Intensity Work
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Badminton repeatedly alternates short high-intensity exchanges with brief recovery, so tactics must manage when to spend acceleration, jump, and lunge resources.
physical_demands.training_signal: Condition tactical drills around rally-rest timing instead of only steady-state conditioning.

physical_demands.name: Visual Anticipation and Fast Reads
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Players must read shuttle trajectory, racket preparation, opponent body shape, partner position, and open court under time pressure.
physical_demands.training_signal: Use live opponent feeds, disguise recognition, and decision constraints more than closed repetition alone.

physical_demands.name: Lunges, Braking, and Direction Changes
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Net play, late defense, and corner-to-corner movement depend on high-quality deceleration and re-acceleration.
physical_demands.training_signal: Tactical plans should consider whether the athlete can repeat the movement pattern safely under fatigue.

physical_demands.name: Jump and Overhead Repetition
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Repeated jump smashes and steep attacks can create pressure but may degrade landing, shoulder control, and shot selection when overused.
physical_demands.training_signal: Track high-intensity overhead volume and require tactical variety after repeated smash sequences.

physical_demands.name: Event-Format Specificity
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Singles emphasizes larger court coverage and rally construction; doubles increases shot frequency and formation speed; mixed adds role and rotation stress.
physical_demands.training_signal: Do not use a singles-only drill library to prepare doubles and mixed decision speed.

physical_demands.name: Aerobic and Anaerobic Blend
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Anaerobic bursts create attacks and recoveries; aerobic capacity supports repeated rally recovery and decision quality across games.
physical_demands.training_signal: Pair tactical pressure games with recovery monitoring and repeat-bout quality.

physical_demands.name: Tournament Repeatability
physical_demands.tactical_relevance: Multiple matches in a week or day reduce tolerance for high-risk, high-load patterns unless recovery is managed.
physical_demands.training_signal: Plan lower-volume tactical sharpening, between-match cooldown, and match-specific movement choices.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Knee and Ankle Risk During Direction Change
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Fast braking, wide lunges, recovery turns, and changes of direction are recurring mechanisms for knee and ankle issues.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Avoid repeatedly forcing exhausted athletes into late front-court lunges; use higher lifts, safer depth, or slower tempo when movement quality drops.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Patellar and Achilles Tendon Load
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Repeated jumps, lunges, split steps, and high-speed attacks can accumulate tendon load.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Limit repeated jump-smash and maximal front-back patterns during sore or congested weeks.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Shoulder Overhead Volume
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Smashes, clears, and repeated overhead disguise can stress shoulder structures, especially when fatigue changes mechanics.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Rotate attack options: body smash, half smash, drop, clear, and net follow rather than maximal smash repetition.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Low Back Rotation and Extension Load
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Rear-court overheads, round-the-head shots, emergency defense, and repeated trunk rotation can load the low back.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: If back symptoms rise, reduce forced round-the-head patterns and use footwork or shot choices that avoid repeated late trunk extension.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Wrist and Elbow Reactive Exchange Load
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Fast drives, late defensive blocks, deceptive slices, and grip changes can stress wrist and elbow tissues when volume spikes.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Use shot-menu variety and recovery days after high-volume drive or deception sessions.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Fatigue Decision-Injury Cascade
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Fatigue increases late contact, poor recovery, rushed shot selection, and repeated emergency movements.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: In training, stop or regress tactical games when decision quality and movement quality both drop.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Tournament Congestion
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Multiple matches and short recovery windows increase accumulated lunge, jump, overhead, and cognitive load.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Prefer simple high-percentage plans, controlled warm-ups, between-match recovery, and lower-risk movement patterns when fatigue accumulates.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Surface and Footwear Risk
injury_or_load_risks.risk_context: Court grip, slippery floors, and footwear issues can change braking safety and shot-choice risk.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_adjustment: Adapt margin, lunge depth, and jump attack frequency when traction is uncertain.

training_implications.implication: Use score-start drills from 0-0, 8-8, 16-16, 19-19, and game point to train tactical risk choices under specific pressure states.
Train serve, receive, and third shot as a linked micro-rally with live scoring and formation accountability.
For intermediate and advanced players, code first-three outcomes from match video to identify whether errors come from serve quality, receive intent, third-shot coverage, or rotation.
Use constrained games that reward moving the opponent and recovering to base before finishing.
Teach rotation through live formation-transition games rather than static position diagrams.
Mixed pairs should rehearse primary roles and emergency role inversion so a single lift or scramble does not break the pair.
Connect attacking shape, defensive shape, and counterattack conversion in one drill cycle.
Build decision drills where the feeder or defender changes position after the player's preparation, forcing a live read instead of a pre-called shot.
Grade deception by whether it preserves balance and next-base recovery, not by how dramatic it looks.
Train athletes to change tempo on purpose: early flat pressure, high reset, slow drop, stick smash, and sudden acceleration.
Develop a simple observation sheet around space, time, strengths, weaknesses, psychology, and pattern causes before using complex analytics.
Beginner teaching should use simple attacking, neutral, and defensive situations with large targets and clear questions.
Intermediate players should learn first-three plans, rally construction, simple scouting, score-state risk, and doubles/mixed formation changes.
Advanced players should train opponent-specific menus, deception under pressure, tempo manipulation, event-specific analytics, and match-week adaptation.
Physical drills should end in tactical decisions, and tactical drills should preserve realistic movement, rally-rest, and event-format demands.
Monitor high-risk tactical volume: jump smashes, late lunges, repeated round-the-heads, flat drive exchanges, and tournament-like multi-match days.
Return from injury should rebuild tactical exposure in stages: controlled placement, planned movement, live read, pressure score, then tournament density.
Backend logging should tag event format, score band, serve/receive state, first-three outcome, formation, opponent position, pressure state, and load-risk marker.

backend_records_to_create.summary: Deep tactical knowledge for score pressure, serve/receive, first-three shots, singles construction, doubles/mixed formations, deception, tempo, match-week planning, physical-tactical demands, and load-risk constraints.

backend_records_to_create.name: Score-State Tactical Risk
backend_records_to_create.rule: Match tactical risk to score band: probe early, consolidate middle-game leads, simplify at end-game, and use rehearsed routines at deuce or match point.

backend_records_to_create.name: Serve-Receive Plus Third Shot
backend_records_to_create.rule: Serve and receive work must include the next two decisions so players understand whether they created attack, stayed neutral, or conceded pressure.

backend_records_to_create.name: Singles Construct Before Finish
backend_records_to_create.rule: Singles players should use width, depth, height, and tempo to create finishing chances before committing to high-risk attacks.

backend_records_to_create.name: Doubles Formation Transition
backend_records_to_create.rule: Doubles pairs should transition between front-back attack, side-by-side defense, and staggered neutral shape based on shuttle height, pressure state, and player momentum.

backend_records_to_create.name: Mixed Doubles Responsibility Roles
backend_records_to_create.rule: Store mixed roles by tactical responsibility and current position rather than fixed gender assumptions; include emergency role inversion.

backend_records_to_create.name: Deception From Balance
backend_records_to_create.rule: Teach deception only when the athlete has a credible base shot, balanced contact, and a recovery plan.

backend_records_to_create.name: Tempo Control
backend_records_to_create.rule: Use speed to punish late opponents, height to reset when late, and pace changes to break anticipation.

backend_records_to_create.name: Match-Week Tactical Sharpening
backend_records_to_create.rule: In match week, rehearse known serve-return menus, pressure score states, event-format rotations, venue adaptation, and recovery rather than installing complex new patterns.

backend_records_to_create.name: Between-Match Tactical Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.rule: Between matches, recover first, then reduce scouting or self-review to one or two actionable changes.

backend_records_to_create.name: Tactical Load Risk Control
backend_records_to_create.rule: Cap or rotate high-risk tactical exposures when fatigue or pain affects movement: repeated jump smashes, late lunges, round-the-heads, and high-speed drive exchanges.

backend_records_to_create.name: Beginner Tactical IQ Progression
assessment_signals: can name attacking or defensive situation

backend_records_to_create.name: Advanced Tactical IQ Progression
assessment_signals: uses two or three match-changing observations
creates front-court control in doubles or mixed

backend_records_to_create.name: Score-State Decision Assessment
backend_records_to_create.assessment_protocol: Play scored points from 8-8, 16-16, 19-19, and match point; player must state serve/receive plan and post-rally adjustment.

backend_records_to_create.name: Serve-Receive Edge Assessment
backend_records_to_create.assessment_protocol: Track 20 serve/receive sequences and code whether each creates attack, stays neutral, concedes defense, or errors.

backend_records_to_create.name: Singles Rally Construction Assessment
backend_records_to_create.assessment_protocol: Play live singles where a point counts double if won after a deliberate front-back or side-side construction pattern.

backend_records_to_create.name: Doubles Rotation Integrity Assessment
backend_records_to_create.assessment_protocol: Use live rallies starting from lift, smash defense, and flat drive exchange; code formation switch, seam coverage, and avoidable collisions.

backend_records_to_create.name: Deception With Recovery Assessment
backend_records_to_create.assessment_protocol: Player uses a base shot and deceptive alternative from the same preparation, then must recover and win or neutralize the next shot.

backend_records_to_create.name: Singles Tactical Builder
responsibilities: move opponent through width and depth
common_errors: repeating same pattern after opponent adapts

backend_records_to_create.name: Doubles Front Player
common_errors: standing too close after loose attack
not recovering after being lifted over

backend_records_to_create.name: Doubles Rear Player
common_errors: forcing cross attacks from late contact

backend_records_to_create.name: Mixed Front-Court Controller
common_errors: assuming partner always handles rear scramble

backend_records_to_create.name: Mixed Rear-Court Pressure Player
common_errors: failing to reset shape after scramble

backend_records_to_create.name: Serve-Return Edge
backend_records_to_create.definition: Net first-three-shot advantage: attack or forced lift created minus direct first-three errors.

backend_records_to_create.name: Forced Lift Rate
backend_records_to_create.definition: Percentage of tactical sequences where the player or pair forces the opponent to lift from serve-return, net pressure, or attack.

backend_records_to_create.name: Attack Conversion
backend_records_to_create.definition: Points or decisive advantage won after obtaining downward attack.

backend_records_to_create.name: Rotation Integrity
backend_records_to_create.definition: Rate of doubles or mixed rallies without avoidable collision, double chase, uncovered seam, or delayed formation transition.

backend_records_to_create.name: Pressure Error Rate
backend_records_to_create.definition: Decision or execution errors by score band, especially after intervals, at 16-plus, deuce, game point, and match point.

backend_records_to_create.name: Deception Quality
backend_records_to_create.definition: Successful delayed-read actions that preserve the player's balance and produce advantage on the current or next shot.

backend_records_to_create.name: Late Lunge Cluster
backend_records_to_create.trigger: Multiple late or unstable lunges in a short drill or match window.
backend_records_to_create.recommended_adjustment: Regress to higher-margin clears, reduced court width, controlled net entries, or end the high-intensity block.

backend_records_to_create.name: Jump Smash Volume
backend_records_to_create.trigger: Repeated high-intensity jump smashes, especially in match week or with landing quality decline.
backend_records_to_create.recommended_adjustment: Switch to half-smash, stick smash, drop, clear variation, or front-court pressure patterns.
